item.title: Cameroon’s Aging President Returns From Monthslong Stay Abroad
item.description:
After two and a half months abroad, President Paul Biya returned to Cameroon on Thursday, according to state media, as questions mounted about his health and succession plans.

Since assuming office in 1982, Mr. Biya has become known for frequent stays overseas, where he has amassed hotel bills that by some estimates have reached into the millions of dollars.

The Cameroonian authorities banned public discussions of the strongman ruler’s health in 2024 as speculation surrounding his absences grew. During his latest stint overseas in Switzerland, the president issued official statements but did not appear on camera or clarify the purpose of what his office called “a brief private stay.”

On Thursday afternoon, Mr. Biya’s plane landed in Yaoundé, the capital, the state broadcaster Cameroon Radio Television reported. Brief footage, which could not be independently verified, showed Mr. Biya shaking hands with officials before stepping into a car.

The state broadcaster televised large crowds of people singing and dancing outside of the airport, many of them wearing clothes printed with the faces of Mr. Biya and his wife, Chantal, who is also an influential public figure.

While Mr. Biya was away, Cameroon continued to grapple with armed conflict and political uncertainty. A militant secessionist movement in the English-speaking regions of the country is in its tenth year. Threats also loomed in the far north, where extremists affiliated with the Islamic State attacked villages earlier this year, seeking to expand their influence.

And more recently, a deadly landslide on Tuesday at a mine in the neighboring Central African Republic killed 100 people, including several Cameroonian miners.

Some Cameroonian analysts and journalists have said that the president’s most recent trip was among his longest and most troubling. This latest stint “weakened the perception of him as a genuine leader attached to his people and his country,” said Christopher Fomunyoh, the regional director for Central and West Africa Programs at the National Democratic Institute for International Affairs, a nonprofit organization in Washington.

Rumors have swirled in Yaoundé about succession battles behind the scenes among the president’s family and close advisers, analysts said. Contenders vying to assume control may include the president’s son Franck Biya and stepson Franck Hertz, the son of Chantal Biya, the influential first lady, said Manu Lekunze, a lecturer in international relations at the University of Aberdeen in Scotland. Tensions between factions within Mr. Biya’s political party are also likely to come to the fore once Mr. Biya’s reign ends, Mr. Fomunyoh said.

In April, Cameroon’s Parliament approved a constitutional amendment re-establishing the role of vice president, whose occupant would take power in the event of the president’s death, resignation or inability to hold office. But Mr. Biya has refused to anoint a potential rival by naming someone for the position, some experts said.

“The reason why he hasn’t appointed vice president is because he knows that if he sets out a clear pathway to succession, then it makes it much easier for people to kick him aside,” Mr. Lekunze said.

Mr. Biya extended his rule in a disputed presidential election in 2025. The government responded to opposition protests with mass arrests and lethal force, according to Human Rights Watch.

Mr. Biya is one of many aging, long-ruling leaders in Africa. Excluding monarchs, four of the five longest-serving current heads of state are in Africa. Mr. Biya is the oldest sitting president and has the second longest tenure, outranked only by President Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo of Equatorial Guinea.

item.title: Mark Zuckerberg Buys an Irish Castle
item.description:
For two centuries, Strancally Castle’s towers and parapets have overlooked a bend in the Blackwater River and a swath of Irish land as it passed from one wealthy family to the next.

It now joins the holdings of Mark Zuckerberg, one of the 21st century’s most prominent landowners, along with a place on an artificial island in Miami Beach, a large house in Washington and compounds in California and Hawaii.

A spokesman for Mr. Zuckerberg, the 42-year-old billionaire chief executive of Meta, confirmed this week that he had bought the castle, a Gothic-style estate in Waterford County, a region of southeastern Ireland with about 130,000 people. The castle was built around 1830 and renovated in the early 2000s.

The purchase does not appear to be listed in Ireland’s ​property price register. The Irish Times, which reported the news on Thursday, estimated that the estate could be worth $23 million to $35 million.

Around the middle of the 19th century, the estate was valued at 61 pounds, according to an entry about the castle in a University of Galway archive of landed estates that also mentions it contained an art collection and a library.

“Mark and his family look forward to caring for this historic home and visiting when traveling to Ireland,” said Brian Baker, the spokesman for Mr. Zuckerberg.

The castle was built for a former member of Parliament, John Keily, according to Ireland’s National Built Heritage Service, which describes the building as both “muscular” and “dour.”

The estate has never left private hands, leaving the public to glimpse its interior only in historical archives. An entry about Mr. Keily in “The History of Parliament” website says the house was designed “on a lavish scale; it took a brisk walk of 4½ minutes to reach the dining room from the kitchen.”

The castle was most recently owned by Michael Alen-Buckley, the chairman of the investment firm RAB Capital, and his wife, Giancarla Alen-Buckley, a member of the family behind the luxury Rocco Forte Hotels group.

“We leave our home of twenty-five years fondly and are grateful for the opportunity we have been given to save and restore Strancally Castle,” the couple said in a statement. “We are delighted that Mark and his family intend to build on our stewardship by continuing to invest in maintaining and enhancing the property and grounds as their home.”

It is not clear how much time Mr. Zuckerberg or his family (he has three daughters with his wife, Priscilla Chan) will spend in Ireland, but his company has a significant presence there.

Like many major U.S. companies, Meta uses an office in Dublin as its European headquarters, and about 1,500 employees work there. Ireland has become a hub for multinational corporations, both for its relatively low corporate income tax rate, 15 percent for big companies, and its history of allowing corporations to shift profits out of the country into places like Bermuda, Grand Cayman and the Isle of Man.

Ireland’s status as a base for several technological giants has made it a key player in enforcing European Union regulations and, increasingly, a center of protest against the companies and their data centers.

Asked for comment about Mr. Zuckerberg’s purchase, the Waterford City and County Council extolled the area’s attractions — wild coastlines and mountains, picturesque festivals and towns — and the history of the county and city.

“Founded by the Vikings in 914 AD, Waterford is Ireland’s Oldest City that has been shaped by centuries of history and today it is evident that the county’s remarkable architecture keeps its past vividly present,” the council said in an email.

“We hope that Mr. Zuckerberg and his family fully enjoy all that Waterford has to offer.”

item.title: Sun Screen
item.description:
I saw “E.T.” at a drive-in movie theater on Cape Cod in the summer of 1982. The film itself takes place in fall (remember when they cloak E.T. in a sheet so they can take him trick-or-treating?) but it’s forever suspended in summer for me, inextricable from the sticky back seat and the sticky humidity in which I saw it. But “Die Hard,” which was released in the summer of 1988, takes place on Christmas Eve and — for me at least — is a winter movie. I’m sure I saw it the July it came out, but the film’s content transcends its summer blockbuster status.

What makes a movie a summer movie? In 2000, Terrence Rafferty declared in The Times, “Steven Spielberg’s ‘Jaws’ created the Summer Movie as we know it: the action-heavy ‘thrill ride’ sort of picture, aimed at sensation-hungry younger audiences, which moves into theaters around Memorial Day and remains there, partying hard, until the school year starts up again in September.” “Jaws” continues to be as bound up in the mythology of summer as Popsicles and beach balls, though a piece by Stuart Klawans in 2002 blamed it for turning the beach into “a site of isolation, anxiety and horror,” one that foreclosed the insouciance of “Beach Blanket Bingo” and its ilk, and gave way to “Cast Away,” “Titanic” and other pessimistic seaborne tales. (Those each came out in December, for what it’s worth.)

When I think about the movies that unfailingly evoke summer for me, I think of a feeling, a quality of light, an airy mood of expansiveness. The exemplar is the 1988 comedy “Mystic Pizza,” starring Julia Roberts, Lili Taylor and Annabeth Gish as three charming, brave, wisecracking pals working at their local Connecticut pizzeria the summer after high school. They each fall in love. They each have their hearts cracked, if not totally broken. They each presented to me, 14 when I first saw the movie, a romantic vision of what summer might look like when I was older, when I would have a job and go on dates and have my own heart broken.

When I asked people about their quintessential summer films, the answers weren’t surprising, but, aside from “Jaws,” they also weren’t Big Movies. They were the ones with an atmosphere of summer, the ones whose mentions fairly conjure the itch of a mosquito bite and the smell of a bonfire: “Meatballs.” “Little Darlings.” “Dirty Dancing.” “Do the Right Thing.” They’re films that, no matter when you watch them, transport you to some deliciously unattainable past. Unlike songs of summer, which are artifacts of one specific year, movies of summer are perennial, evocative of every summer all at once.

I haven’t seen anything yet this year that feels like it’ll enter the pantheon of eternal summer classics. “The Odyssey” probably isn’t a worthy contender, as entertaining as it is. But I’m planning to see “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” this week, which seems like it might hold genuine promise.

Trade

The United States will impose new tariffs on some $20 billion worth of Canadian goods, on top of hefty tariffs already in place on major Canadian industries, after the two countries failed to reach a deal before a midnight deadline.

President Trump announced that he would allow ground beef to be imported into the U.S. with lower tariffs over the next 90 days. The news seemed to surprise and anger American ranchers.

Trump Administration

Chief Justice John Roberts said Trump could continue building his White House ballroom, for now, while the Supreme Court considers the case.

Trump threatened to sue a liberal think tank for $5 billion for reporting that his National Guard deployments had little effect on reducing violent crime.

The Trump administration has sharply slowed funding to Harvard University via the National Institutes of Health, despite a court ruling forcing the administration to undo cuts.

Immigration

A private prison company donated more than $1.4 million to Trump’s PAC shortly after the company was awarded lucrative government contracts to house immigrants awaiting deportation.

The Trump administration approved a $5 million payment to Liberia in connection with a deal to send migrants there, internal documents show.

At least five migrants deported to Liberia refused to get off the plane there. They were then taken to another country, Equatorial Guinea.

More Politics

The Pentagon fired the publisher and the editor in chief of Stars and Stripes, a government-funded news outlet that covers the military, after it reported on deteriorating morale on the U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln.

A Times exclusive: Jessica Ramos, a New York state senator, has used campaign funds for travel while billing taxpayers for the same charges.

Middle East

A top Iranian official said the country would seek to dampen the effect of economic sanctions after the Trump administration vowed to aggressively tighten them.

The risk of a catastrophic oil spill in the Strait of Hormuz has increased as tankers navigate the waterway with their location devices turned off.

A Palestinian teenager was killed after Israeli settlers entered a village in the West Bank. The Palestinian and the Israeli authorities offered conflicting accounts of the incident.

Other Big Stories

TikTok agreed to pay $400 million to settle a lawsuit brought by the Justice Department during the Biden administration concerning the company’s collection of data from users under the age of 13.

Much of Gary, Ind., has been without electricity for 10 days since deadly storms ripped through the city.

Mark Zuckerberg bought an Irish castle.

Giorgia Meloni reflected on her route from onetime outcast to prime minister of Italy in a rare interview with The Times. (Read takeaways.)

Film and TV

The year of the sex mentor: In recent films, including “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” and “The Invite,” middle-aged gurus are helping younger characters relearn desire.

Two (unrelated) movies about guys on a chaotic road trip — one called “Nimrods,” the other “Idiots” — are hitting theaters this month. Here’s how that happened.

“It Ends,” a horror film about a road trip with no exit, is a taut, efficient thriller about the transition into adulthood, our critic writes.

Music

With the Kennedy Center shuttered for a two-year renovation, the National Symphony Orchestra plans to perform in six halls scattered across the Washington area. It will also embark on its first national tour in years.

Ye, the rapper formerly known as Kanye West, is set to perform two stadium shows in St. Petersburg, Russia, this fall. The concerts would be the first in Russia by a major Western performer since the invasion of Ukraine.

More Culture

A production of “Les Misérables” at Tuacahn in southern Utah, staged outdoors against the region’s dramatic landscape, may be the most successful in the theater’s 31-year history. Michael Paulson, a theater reporter, traveled there to explain why. Click the video above to watch.

Our dance critic writes about the champion surfer Caitlin Simmers: “Surfing can be an art, motion turned into magic. Simmers takes that a step further by matching her personal rhythm to that of the sea.” Read her profile.

Rachel Cusk’s new novel, “Life of M,” is full of details that echo the life and career of Natalie Portman — though the writer refuses to concede that it’s about her. It left our critic cold.

By Melissa Clark

Easy to make but hard to stop eating, Melissa Knific’s golden, vegetable-filled zucchini fritters are a great place to use up all the summer squash that’s in season right now. The trick here is to squeeze the zucchini in a kitchen towel to remove all the excess moisture. This ensures that they turn crispy as they fry, rather than steam. Serve them with something tangy on the side — either lemon wedges for squeezing or a punchy sauce like ranch dressing or tzatziki for dipping.

The Hunt: A pair of empty-nesters decided to relocate to Portugal, but Lisbon had become too expensive. A nearby coastal city won them over. Which home did they choose? Play our game.

On the water: When three generations of the Schipper family escape their urban homes to gather at Lake Rosseau in Ontario, they don’t just live near the water — they live on it, in a boathouse.

Miami millions: For the first time, living in South Florida costs more than living in the New York City area.

Exhibit A: West Palm Beach has long been a working-class city. A single developer’s $10 billion construction plan is changing that identity.

Vintage, baby: Parents have long dressed their children in hand-me-downs. But lately some are seeking items with a rarer provenance, and prices are becoming stratospheric.

It’s still summer: A swim in wild waters can bring escape and exhilaration. Here are six places on state and national park land to backstroke, butterfly or just beat the heat.

Melanoma F.A.Q.: This week, Merck and Moderna announced promising results from a clinical trial for an mRNA vaccine to treat melanoma. Here is the latest on what doctors know about the skin cancer.

Always changing: Our writer noticed her feet had suddenly grown a size. Turns out, it’s a common sign of aging. Here are four other unexpected changes.

There are no universal guidelines for how to nurture kids’ relationships with technology, but after interviewing experts, combing through research and surveying hundreds of Wirecutter readers with kids under 18, we’ve compiled some advice — including when to introduce your teen to social media. Before setting up an account, start an open dialogue about how the algorithm works and how it can affect the way they feel. Turn on privacy settings. And remind your teen that future employers or college-admissions officers may look at their social media, so they should be cautious about what they post. Finally, build trust so they feel comfortable coming to you if they interact with something or someone troubling. — Ellen Lee

Here is today’s Spelling Bee. Yesterday’s pangram was groundhog.

And here are today’s Mini Crossword, Wordle, Crossplay, Connections and Strands.

item.title: Missing From a Mass Wedding in India: Brides
item.description:
Abhishek Varma could not shake the feeling that something was wrong on his wedding day.

His parents, desperate to marry him off, had found a man in a nearby village in India who described himself as a matchmaker. All they had to do, he told them, was select an orphaned woman from a photo album and pay around $200 to join a mass wedding.

When the day came in late May, Mr. Varma and about 40 other grooms from several villages arrived at 8 a.m. in wedding kurtas and sherwanis, he said. They waited all day for their brides — until they realized they’d been duped.

“They took the bait,” said Preeti Katare, a police officer handling the case, adding that the victims were rural men in their early 20s to 40s. She added that dozens of others had not come forward out of shame.

The case — in which the purported matchmaker and his accomplices now face fraud charges in the central state of Madhya Pradesh — is an extreme example of a wedding scam in a marriage industry that is notoriously prone to it.

Many scammers in India are lured by the huge sums of money flowing to its marriage market, in which families spend years saving up for a daughter’s wedding clothing, jewelry and dowry — the traditional, yet illegal, payment of cash or assets to the groom. Marriage scams are common enough that Indian newspapers run full-page ads with tips on how to avoid them.

But fraudulent mass weddings are rare. Ram Lal Bhagat, a sub inspector with the Madhya Pradesh Police, said it was the first one he had seen in 40 years on the job.

About a dozen of the victims, including Mr. Varma, filed complaints that led to the purported matchmaker’s arrest and detention in the central state of Madhya Pradesh. In late July, the police there said they had charged the man, Dinesh Bairagi, 45, and four accomplices, including his brother, Mukesh Bairagi, 40.

A lawyer for the Bairagis could not be reached for comment. If convicted, they could face a punishment of up to three years in prison and a fine.

The police said that the Bairagis reaped the equivalent of around $4,000 by charging each man 10,000 to 25,000 rupees ($105 to $260), a significant sum for rural families but a bargain price for a wedding. They “saw an opportunity in this problem where it’s hard for a lower- to middle-income groom to find a bride in a village setting,” Ms. Katare said.

For Abhishek Varma’s parents, arranging his marriage to an orphan was a way to end his relationship with another woman, the daughter of a chauffeur.

Because he was the unemployed son of a farmer from a lower caste, he said, his girlfriend’s parents thought he had little to offer her and threatened to harm his family if the couple did not separate.

Mr. Varma said his family pressured him to choose a bride based on photos of women in an orphanage, and that the matchmakers declined to let him meet her before the wedding.

“They said it was not the rule of the orphanage to have the girls meet strange men like that,” he said in a phone interview. “I had slight doubts, but I had no option but to go along with my family. Honor is everything.”

Mr. Varma, who has a computer science degree but works odd jobs, said that some of his fellow grooms were unemployed young men like him, while others were in their 40s and 50s and considered too old for the marriage market.

More than 5 percent of men in India are unemployed, according to the Ministry of Statistics and Program Implementation, a figure that experts say does not account for the country’s sprawling informal sector. A March report by Azim Premji University in Bengaluru found that nearly 40 percent of recent graduates were unemployed.

Indian families typically prefer to marry their daughters to men who come from a different caste or have a high earning potential, to justify the cost of a wedding and a dowry, said Gaurav Chiplunkar, a business professor at the University of Virginia who has studied rural India’s marriage market. Those women tend to leave their villages, leaving local men behind.

“The marriage market is so skewed that there are just no brides, or the men are older, or they need women to work in the household while the men go to their jobs in the cities,” he said.

Matching a son to an orphaned woman typically indicates that a family is desperate enough to forego a dowry, which would provide a financial buffer for the groom’s family if he were unemployed, Professor Chiplunkar said.

India’s Parliament passed a law banning dowries in 1961, but the payments are still common and can cost hundreds of dollars, the equivalent of years of income for a rural bride’s family, according to Professor Chiplunkar’s research.

To remedy the shortage of brides, state governments offer financial incentives for mass weddings, which are typically shorter and cheaper than traditional ones that last for days. In Uttar Pradesh, for example, the bride receives around $600 in cash and about $250 worth of wedding paraphernalia. The state’s chief minister said in 2024 that around 400,000 women from poor and ethnic minority families had been married through the program.

State-sponsored mass weddings often take place before key elections. In 2022, Prime Minister Narendra Modi took a break from campaigning in his home state of Gujarat to attend a wedding for more than 500 women who had lost their fathers.

But the fraudulent mass wedding in Madhya Pradesh was not connected to a government program or an election. The police said the family behind it used their reputation in the village to gain their victims’ trust.

“In villages, trust works,” Ms. Katare said. “And they trusted this family.”

As the hours ticked by without any sign of their brides, the celebratory mood gave way to anger. The grooms and their families restlessly paced around the temple in Dewas, the small city where the purported matchmaker had told them to gather.

Around 5 p.m., Mr. Varma said there was a collective sigh of relief when a man from the Bairagi family arrived with more men from his village. They thought it meant that other Bairagis would soon arrive with their brides.

Their relief did not last long: The police were called to the temple soon after dark.

Mr. Varma said he later looked into the photos of the women provided by the matchmakers. They were not orphans, he said, but influencers who had millions of followers on Instagram.

As for his former girlfriend, he said, she is happy that his wedding didn’t work out.

item.title: Yvette Roudy, France’s First Minister for Women’s Rights, Dies at 97
item.description:
Yvette Roudy, a tenacious feminist who successfully championed state reimbursement for abortions in her role as France’s first minister of women’s rights, died on Tuesday in Cabestany, outside Perpignan, on the Mediterranean coast of France. She was 97.

Her death, at a nursing home, was announced by President Emmanuel Macron of France, who saluted her for “a life spent making equality between men and women a real right” and for her “untiring capacity for indignation.”

The 1982 law that Ms. Roudy (pronounced ROO-dee) supported, guaranteeing that women’s abortions would be covered by France’s national medical insurance, united two of her passions: the rights of women and the fight against economic inequality.

Abortion had been legal in France since 1975, but it was available only to women with the means to seek it. That rankled Ms. Roudy, a lifelong Socialist with a working-class background. And as the woman in charge of a newly created ministry, she could do something about it.

“I thought, since this law existed,” she recalled in a 2008 interview with France Culture radio, referring to the 1975 law legalizing abortion, “it should be open to everyone, not just those who could afford it.”

She added: “This was an inequality requiring a measure of social justice.”

Every week for months, she said, she hounded the new French president, her longtime ally François Mitterrand, reminding him of his campaign promise to reimburse women for their abortions, even as the Roman Catholic Church lobbied him in an attempt to thwart her.

“He was very annoyed,” Ms. Roudy said, but “he finally gave in.”

That persistence was the hallmark of a career that began unpromisingly, under the thumb of a chauvinist father, in Ms. Roudy’s telling. Her feminism, she said, sprang from her early resistance to the status quo — an inequality between the sexes that felt stifling in the small town outside Bordeaux where she grew up.

“I had to become what I eventually became on my own,” she told France Culture.

Ms. Roudy’s two other major initiatives under Mr. Mitterrand encountered mixed success. A 1983 law calling for professional parity between the sexes — in hiring and salaries — remained largely “a dead letter,” the newspaper Libération wrote this week. There was no enforcement mechanism, Ms. Roudy said in a 2019 interview with Le Parisien, and employers “had no desire to enforce it.”

She had better luck with her determination to make contraception more widely available, bringing the issue to the attention of every French household with an advertisement directed by the filmmaker Agnès Varda that was broadcast on prime-time television. Again, the Catholic Church lobbied against her.

But she knew what she was up against. “Machismo in France is stronger,” she told The New York Times in 1985, comparing the situation in her own country unfavorably with what she thought prevailed in the United States.

Even so, she was dismissive of the idea that condescending treatment of women was simply a matter of culture — French culture, specifically.

“I have no idea if there is such a thing as ‘French gallantry,’ and to tell you the truth, I’m not in the least bit interested,” she told the magazine Le Nouvel Obs in 2018. “What I want is for men to stop rubbing themselves up against women in the metro, among other things, and that they stop thinking they are naturally superior.”

Yvette Saldou was born on April 10, 1929, in Pessac, the youngest of three children of Jeanne (Dicharry) Saldou and Joseph Saldou, a metalworker who had been disabled by injuries in World War I and was employed by the municipal government.

When Yvette was 12, her mother died. Under pressure from her father, who saw no need for her to pursue further education, she left school at 16 to work as a secretary at a local fish-processing factory. She began studying at night for her baccalauréat — roughly equivalent to a high school diploma and all-important in France — and finally obtained it at 26.

In 1951, she married Pierre Roudy, a teacher who later became the head of one of France’s national theater schools, and they moved to Scotland, where he had obtained a teaching job.

She learned English as well, and when they returned to France in 1955, she became friendly with the feminist Colette Audry. In 1964, Ms. Audry suggested that Ms. Roudy translate “The Feminine Mystique,” Betty Friedan’s recently published and hugely influential book expressing the frustrations of women who felt trapped or subordinated in domestic roles.

“I was already a feminist, by intuition,” she told Libération in 2019. “But doing this translation allowed me to give words to what I was feeling deep inside.”

Through Ms. Audry, she met Mr. Mitterrand, who was running as a Socialist in a failed bid for the presidency in 1965, and her own career in politics began. Ms. Roudy was serving as a Socialist deputy in the European Parliament by the time Mr. Mitterrand finally became president in 1981 and appointed her as the women’s rights minister, a position that she held until 1986.

Afterward, she went on to serve two stints as a member of the French Parliament from the Calvados department in Normandy, from 1988 to 1993 and from 1997 to 2002. She also served as the mayor of the Norman town Lisieux from 1989 to 2001.

Mr. Roudy died in 2012. Ms. Roudy has no immediate survivors.

After she left government service, Ms. Roudy continued to be regularly consulted by successors to the ministerial position she had held and by journalists eager for her views on the progress of women in France. The #MeToo movement, she told Le Nouvel Obs in 2018, was “making the patriarchy tremble.”

But she hadn’t lost her hardheaded realism about who was calling the shots in French politics.

As she had observed on the television program “Apostrophes” more than three decades earlier, when her book “À Cause d’Elles” (loosely translated as “Thanks to the Women”) came out, “All the rules have been dictated by men. They made all this stuff up in the back rooms of bistros.”

Alain Delaquérière and Daphné Anglès contributed research.

item.title: Waking Up to an Escalating Canada-U.S. Trade War
item.description:
Even by the standards of the Trump administration it was an up and down week. On Tuesday President Trump declared that a trade deal with Canada had been reached. Late Friday night, Prime Minister Mark Carney blamed last minute American demands as he ordered his negotiators to walk away from the table and return to Ottawa.

Now Canada and the United States, two former partners in free trade, are locked in a high stakes trade war that escalated sharply last night. Washington has imposed 50 percent tariffs on what it estimates to be $20 billion in Canadian goods. Mr. Carney vowed to match them “dollar for dollar.”

[Read: Canada-U.S. Trade War Escalates as Talks Collapse]

[Read: The Topsy-Turvy World of Trump’s Canada Tariffs]

[Read: Trump Tariff Talks Leave Key Canadian Official Hopeful]

[Read: Tariffs on Hold as Trump Claims Deal With Canada Is Near]

This week’s tumult over trade in Washington, and the failed negotiations, echo the talks that brought free trade between Canada and the United States in 1989 that transformed Canada’s economy.

Early in my career I was sent by Maclean’s, which was then a weekly newsmagazine, to report on the negotiations in Washington, which began in 1986.

The circumstances then were dramatically different. The initiative came from Canada. And Prime Minister Brian Mulroney and President Ronald Reagan had a close rapport — matched only by Prime Minister Justin Trudeau’s with President Barack Obama decades later.

As Ontario’s recent television ads aired in the United States reminded viewers, Reagan was also a proponent of free trade.

Above all, there was no threat looming over the talks like the sweeping 50 percent tariffs Trump has now imposed after threatening them in July. If the talks failed, there were no potentially disastrous repercussions.

This time around, Janice Charette, a retired public servant who is Canada’s chief negotiator, never speaks when she goes in and out of the Office of the United States Trade Representative, its exterior remarkably unchanged since the 1980s.

That’s in stark contrast with Simon Reisman, Canada’s negotiator back then, also a former public servant who was pulled out of retirement. He was often combative with the reporters, including me, who clustered like pigeons outside the trade office. Most famously, he once called The Toronto Star — which was overtly campaigning against free trade — a “rag,” walked away and then turned around to jab his finger at its correspondent and say, “You are a hack!”

The issues that were difficult to negotiate back then are still with us: softwood lumber; automobiles; Canada’s closed supply management market for dairy; and provincial liquor stores discriminating against American products. There’s the media: Then, it was the United States complaining about Canadian cable systems’ use of American TV signals without compensation; now, it is Canada trying to get American tech giants to pay for Canadian media.

But the biggest sticking point of all was that Canada wanted some sort of independent and binding system that would settle trade disputes between the two countries. Even back then, softwood lumber tariffs — spurred by complaints from American producers that Canada’s forestry system was an unfair subsidy — were a major irritant in the negotiations.

The idea that the United States would suspend its domestic trade laws that led to the lumber tariffs remained a non-starter. But Canada continued to push for an additional system that would hold either country to account for breaking the trade agreement.

The American side argued that making the U.S. government accountable to an independent body was unconstitutional and was unlikely to be approved by Congress.

On Sept. 23, 1987, Reisman declared that the talks were over after 16 months because, he said, the Americans had failed to “belly up to the bar.”

But there was a deadline. The Reagan White House, unlike the Trump administration, respected Congress’s power over trade. And the White House’s authority from Congress to negotiate with Canada expired on Oct. 4.

On Oct. 1, Mulroney sent a delegation to meet with James Baker, the Treasury secretary, whom he described as Washington’s “go-to guy.” Joining Baker was Clayton Yeutter, the United States trade representative.

Suddenly there was the possibility of a deal again.

But late on the evening of Oct. 3, Mulroney wrote, the Canadian delegation phoned from the Treasury building in Washington to say that things had again fallen apart. Shortly after they hung up, the former prime minister wrote, Baker came into the delegation’s room, flung down a piece of paper and said: “All right, you can have your goddamn dispute settlement mechanism.” Michael Wilson, Canada’s finance minister, offered a thumbs-up from a window to journalists outside.

The next morning, a Sunday, rather than go to a bike race as planned, I joined other reporters in a gilded hall in the Treasury building for a more conventional announcement.

The end of negotiations, of course, was only a step toward free trade. A federal election in Canada the year after became a de facto referendum on free trade, with the legislation to implement it stuck in the Liberal-dominated Senate.

While the two countries failed to reach a deal on Friday, Mr. Carney said the talks have only been suspended, leaving open the prospect they may rekindle, as they did in 1987. But if not, we will most likely see another round of talks about the future of the trade pact Canadians call the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement.

Ian Austen reports on Canada for The Times. A Windsor, Ontario, native now based in Ottawa, he has reported on the country for two decades. He can be reached at austen@nytimes.com.

Shots rang out at the United States consulate in Toronto in March as two gunmen took turns firing the same weapon at the building and then sped off in a stolen car. Four months later, the consulate was targeted again by another pair of shooters.

The attacks, the police said, exposed an emerging criminal phenomenon: young guns for hire as gig workers in the underworld economy. Vjosa Isai, our reporter based in Toronto, traced some of the accused teenagers to an apartment block in the city. The neighborhood, beleaguered by gang violence, has been thrust into the spotlight after a policeman was killed in June while investigating the guns-for-hire network.

The network resembles a “violence-as-a-service” scheme under investigation in Europe. Young people are recruited into crime on social media, giving the financiers and criminal brokers hiring them more anonymity.

Read the full article.

Night after night, through the defining events of Lloyd Robertson’s epoch — the first moon landing, the fall of the Berlin Wall, the Persian Gulf war, the Sept. 11 attacks and 14 Canadian federal election campaigns — his plain, matter-of-fact delivery rhymed with the national sensibility.

From Opinion: Matt Dinan, a professor at St. Thomas University in New Brunswick, got his students to love a Dostoyevsky classic by falling in love with it himself, he writes.

From Real Estate: Pick your favorite lakefront home in Ontario.

From The Athletic: The Edmonton Marathon finally admitted that it had miscalculated the length of its race. It was a half-mile longer than 26.2 miles.

item.title: Mexican Governor, Accused by U.S. of Helping Cartel, Returns to His Job
item.description:
The Mexican governor accused by U.S. prosecutors of helping a cartel smuggle drugs announced on Friday that he was back in office, defying charges that set off a scandal in Mexico and inflamed tensions with the United States.

The governor, Rubén Rocha Moya, has said he was innocent and the victim of a political attack. Days after the indictment was unsealed in April, he said he would take a “temporary leave of absence” to focus on defending himself.

Three months later, he declared he was back in the governor’s office of Sinaloa state.

“I return to my responsibility as governor of Sinaloa with a clean, held-high conscience and with the strength of the truth on our side,” he said in a lengthy social media post on Friday.

Mr. Rocha’s return was met with widespread opposition. Governors and senators from his political party joined in releasing pointed statements, saying that he had acted alone and stressing the importance of respecting the continuing investigations. One influential Morena politician who had supported Mr. Rocha, Ricardo Monreal, called for him to go back on leave.

In the indictment, Manhattan prosecutors accused Mr. Rocha and nine other current and former Mexican officials, including a sitting national senator, of a broad conspiracy to help the powerful Sinaloa cartel import drugs into the United States. Prosecutors said that Mr. Rocha had accepted bribes and help getting elected in exchange for protecting the cartel, which has terrorized his state and Mexico for years.

Mr. Rocha, 77, is the highest-ranking member of Mexico’s dominant left-wing political party, Morena, to be indicted by the United States. The case against him is the Trump administration’s most significant public step in cracking down on the corruption that it says is at the heart of Mexico’s cartel problem.

The move caused a political crisis for President Claudia Sheinbaum, also of Morena. And it drove a wedge between the U.S. and Mexican governments as they were deepening security cooperation on combating the cartels.

In May, The New York Times reported that U.S. federal prosecutors had been instructed to use terrorism statutes to target Mexican officials believed to be complicit in the narcotics trade.

Mr. Rocha has long been dogged by accusations of protecting the Sinaloa cartel, a prolific supplier of fentanyl and a ruthless purveyor of violence.

Ms. Sheinbaum, who did not host her daily news conference on Friday because she said she had the flu, did not immediately comment on Mr. Rocha’s return. But she has repeatedly said that her government is not protecting the governor, has demanded more proof from U.S. officials about their case and has backed the Mexican authorities conducting their own investigation.

Mexican officials responded to the U.S. government’s extradition request in April by saying it lacked sufficient evidence.

The U.S. Department of Justice and the U.S. attorney’s office for the Southern District of New York, which filed the indictment, did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Friday.

The Mexican interior ministry called Mr. Rocha’s return “a personal decision” and said an investigation by the attorney general’s office was still open.

The Morena party said on Friday that it had no prior knowledge of his return and “distances itself from this decision.” It said it was committed to due process, the investigation and upholding accountability.

At least two former Sinaloa officials have been detained after U.S. indictments: Gerardo Mérida Sánchez, the former state security chief in Sinaloa, turned himself in to the authorities in Arizona in May; and Enrique Díaz, a former state finance official, was arrested in Europe.

By returning to office, Mr. Rocha regained the constitutional immunity granted by his elected position, experts said. He said on Friday that he had asked for the leave of absence because he wanted to participate in the Mexican government’s investigation as an “ordinary citizen” without immunity.

He said he had appeared before the Mexican attorney general’s office and answered questions with “truthfulness.” He pointed to an announcement by the office that stated that there was not yet sufficient evidence to support the U.S. prosecutors’ claims.

He labeled the accusations against him as “false,” attributing them to what he called the “political and interventionist motives of the national and foreign far right.”

He added, “I have committed no crime under our country’s constitutional and legal framework.”

Jorge Álvarez Máynez, a former presidential candidate and current head of the center-left Citizens’ Movement party, denounced Mr. Rocha’s return as a day of “national shame.”

Carlos Pérez Ricart, a left-leaning political commentator and an expert on organized crime at the Center for Economic Research and Teaching, a Mexican research group, called Mr. Rocha’s return a “grave political error.”

“It is one thing to reject Washington dictating guilt, but quite another to assume that Rocha retains the standing to govern Sinaloa,” he wrote on social media. “Governing requires more than just criminal innocence; it demands political authority.”

Mr. Rocha appeared to be undeterred by such criticism. On Friday, he said that not only had he returned to office, but that he intended to fulfill his term, which ends on Oct. 31, 2027.

item.title: Cities Compete in Dizzying ‘Gold Rush’ to Be Japan’s Backup Capital
item.description:
For 158 years, Tokyo has stood as Japan’s glittering capital, a world-famous nexus of food, culture, business and government.

But Tokyo might soon get an understudy. Japan’s legislature recently passed a bill to create a secondary capital that would serve as an alternate center for the government’s operations, ensuring continuity in the case of a natural disaster or other emergency.

With hundreds of millions of dollars potentially in the offing, and the chance for tax breaks, tourism and urban revival, the plan has set off a frenzy in Japan. Thirteen local governments have already entered the race, including the business hub of Osaka, the southern prefecture of Fukuoka and the northern island of Hokkaido. Even the laid-back, mountainous region of Gunma, home to about 1.9 million people, has thrown its hat into the ring.

Mayors and governors have held flashy news conferences to declare their interest. Osaka has even created a mascot for its bid, a talking “welcoming cat” named Nyaniwa Fukumaru.

HOKKAIDO

Sapporo

Japan

GUNMA

Nagoya

Tokyo

FUKUOKA

Osaka

200 mileS

The New York Times

Masashi Kawai, a senior policy officer at the Tokyo Foundation, a think tank, said the competition had the feel of a grand festival: “A ‘don’t-miss-the-Gold-Rush’ mentality has taken hold.”

The idea has divided Japanese citizens. Supporters of the plan say that Japan, long prone to earthquakes, typhoons and floods, must be prepared for the possibility that its government offices in Tokyo could become debilitated. Opponents say the idea is a misguided proposal meant to reward allies of Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi: One of her closest political partners is the Japan Innovation Party, which has worked for years to establish its home base of Osaka as an alternate capital.

It will be up to Ms. Takaichi to crown the winner. No official timeline has been set, but her cabinet is expected to put together a list of requirements for the secondary capital in the next few months.

The idea of a second capital has some precedent in Japanese history. During the Edo period, from 1603 to 1868, Japan had two capitals. Edo, which later became Tokyo, was a political and administrative capital where the shogun ruled. Kyoto was the cultural and spiritual capital, home to the emperor.

In recent decades, the threat posed by natural disasters has led some experts and politicians to revive the idea. Japan is situated along the Pacific “Ring of Fire,” a chain of seismologically active faults encircling the Pacific Ocean. Experts have warned about the possibility of a so-called megaquake in Tokyo and other large cities.

In 2011, a 9.1-magnitude megaquake and tsunami in northeastern Japan killed more than 19,000 people and triggered a nuclear disaster. The quake was a reminder of the vulnerability of Tokyo, which lies about 230 miles southwest from the epicenter.

Designating another capital could also help decentralize Japan’s population and drive economic growth outside the capital. Many people have left rural areas in recent years for jobs and schooling in Tokyo. While the countryside is hollowing out, the population of the Tokyo metropolitan area has grown, rising slightly to 37 million last year.

Experts agree about the threat that natural disasters could pose to Tokyo’s government. But some critics say the plan would do little to address those risks.

Nobuo Sasaki, a professor emeritus at Tokyo’s Chuo University and a former Tokyo official, said the legislation failed to account for important factors like the stability of the ground in the prospective cities.

“It remains entirely unclear what exactly constitutes a ‘secondary capital’ or how it should be developed,” he said.

Opposition lawmakers argue that Osaka, a top contender, is not suitable to serve as an alternate, given its own vulnerability to earthquakes. They have also expressed concern about the costs of building backup structures to house government offices.

Makiko Kishi, a lawmaker for the Constitutional Democratic Party of Japan, said the proposal was “half-baked” and “tainted by partisan maneuvering and the pursuit of vested interests.”

Some experts argue that Japan should focus instead on fortifying Tokyo’s own defenses against earthquakes and other threats. They say that designating a backup capital could also exacerbate problems in rural Japan, causing millions to flee the countryside for another megacity.

Despite the conflicting views, local leaders across Japan have rushed in recent weeks to explain why their regions should be chosen.

In the city of Nagoya, Mayor Ichiro Hirosawa skipped a planned dance festival last month to hold a news conference promoting his city. He has said the city plans to play up its manufacturing prowess and to “do everything in our power to capture the country.”

Officials in the northern prefecture of Hokkaido and its capital, Sapporo City, have set up teams to focus on securing second-capital status. They have emphasized their region’s distance from Nankai Trough, a seismically active zone off southern Japan.

Mr. Kawai, the policy expert, said it would be hard to replicate Tokyo’s success. Regions should instead focus on coming up with creative ways to promote economic growth, he said, to offset the declining population.

“Without that approach,” he said, “the secondary-capital initiative will bring 100 harms and not one good.”

item.title: Canada-U.S. Trade War Escalates as Talks Collapse
item.description:
Crucial trade talks between the United States and Canada to stave off punishing new tariffs by the Trump administration on Canadian goods collapsed late Friday, with Canada saying it would retaliate “dollar for dollar.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada said he had decided to suspend the talks because the American side had introduced last-minute terms that were “unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal.”

He added that the talks, which had been going on for weeks and had intensified in the past few days, had marked important progress but had ultimately “not been enough to meet our objectives for Canadians.”

United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told reporters that Canada had walked away from the negotiating table, minutes before a deadline ushering in new 50 percent tariffs by the Trump administration on a broad range of Canadian goods.

“Tonight, Canada declined to finalize the trade deal under the terms agreed earlier this week, despite the U.S. offer to Canada to receive the best treatment of any major exporter to our market,” Mr. Greer said on a virtual briefing with the press.

“New demands and walk backs of other commitments by Canada have upended the careful balance reached in the past days,” Mr. Greer added.

Shortly before Mr. Greer’s statement to the press, U.S. Customs and Border Protection sent out guidance for importers saying that the Canadian products that the president had identified would face tariffs after 12:01 a.m.

Speaking to reporters, a U.S. official said that Canada wanted concessions that the United States wasn’t prepared to give, particularly when it came to the automotive sector, as well as trade in steel, aluminum and lumber.

If Canada does retaliate, the official said, Mr. Trump would be provided with options “to level out the playing field once again.”

In his statement, Mr. Carney said Canada would retaliate against the new tariffs, which will affect $20 billion in Canadian exports by the U.S. administration’s calculations, “to protect our workers and businesses.”

In addition to making hundreds of Canadian products like cheese and hockey sticks price-prohibitive in the U.S. market, the tariffs will further fracture the once-close relationship between the countries, which has drastically deteriorated since Mr. Trump returned to office, targeted Canada with tariffs and repeatedly proposed that it be annexed as the 51st state.

Negotiators from both countries have been cooped up in the United States trade representative’s office in Washington for up to 10 hours a day for several days this week hammering out the details of the failed agreement.

Just hours before the two sides announced negotiations had been suspended, Mr. Trump said he thought a deal could be reached with Canada. On Tuesday he declared that the two nations had reached a deal aside from working out some details and had extended an earlier deadline that would have introduced the new tariffs.

But Mr. Carney made good on his promise to walk away from a deal he didn’t think was good enough. Polling suggests that many Canadians support his decision. A recent Léger poll found that 56 percent of respondents are opposed to any further trade concessions from Canada.

He also got an early endorsement for his decision to walk away from talks from Doug Ford, the premier of Ontario, Canada’s most populous province and home to the country’s important auto industry. “As we fight to protect Canadian sovereignty and economic security, everything needs to be on the table. Ontario is ready to do its part,” Mr. Ford said.

In addition to fending off the new tariffs, Canada wanted to use the talks to roll back and ideally eliminate tariffs of up to 50 percent that Mr. Trump has imposed on the country’s steel, aluminum and autos. Canadian negotiators also hoped to achieve some relief on softwood lumber tariffs that go back decades and were augmented with additional tariffs from Mr. Trump.

The U.S. side wanted the eight Canadian provinces that had barred American wine and spirits from their government-owned alcohol distribution systems to end the boycotts, which were brought in last year in response to Mr. Trump’s trade attack. It also wanted Canada to drop its retaliatory tariff on American cars and to change how American dairy products are allowed into Canada’s tightly controlled market.

In the final days of negotiations, it appeared that Canada had become resigned to only succeeding in reducing, not eliminating, the current tariffs.

Leading into Friday’s talks, several people in both countries briefed on the negotiations described U.S. proposals that still maintained substantial, if lower, tariffs on the two metals and autos.

They said that the plan would cut steel and aluminum tariffs to 25 percent from 50 percent. But only a limited quantity of Canadian steel would be allowed at that reduced rate, with the balance still facing a 50 percent tariff.

Under the plan, the people briefed said, autos would fall to 15 percent from 25 percent, with the rate being adjusted for American parts, which typically make up about half the value of a vehicle made in Canada. Executives and analysts in the auto industry said that would still leave production in Canada unprofitable and likely doom assembly plants in the country.

While the Supreme Court struck down most of Mr. Trump’s tariffs in February, both last year’s tariffs and the new measures against Canada were brought under other trade laws that were not covered by the decision.

The legal provision that Mr. Trump has used to impose the new 50 percent tariffs on Canada, Section 338, stems from a 1930 law and has never been used before. The tariffs could face legal challenges in the coming weeks.

The development was bad news for consumers and businesses on both sides of the border, warned Candace Laing, who leads the Canadian Chamber of Commerce.

“This will be a body blow to North American competitiveness in this self-defeating trade saga,” she said. “Americans will see their costs go up, and Canadians will see customers, investment and small businesses disappear.”

item.title: How a Trump Envoy Uses Vodka and Dirty Jokes to Conduct U.S. Diplomacy
item.description:
When John Coale, a friend of President Trump’s serving as a diplomat in Eastern Europe, was asked on short notice to meet with Belarus’s strongman leader, Aleksandr G. Lukashenko, he followed colleagues’ advice to “yuk it up.”

It was perhaps a surprising suggestion. The U.S. government had given Mr. Lukashenko the diplomatic cold shoulder after he asked President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia for help in 2020 to violently suppress pro-democracy protests. Mr. Lukashenko further isolated his country by letting Mr. Putin use Belarus as a staging ground for Russia’s invasion of Ukraine two years later.

Still, Mr. Coale gave it a shot, arriving in Belarus’s capital, Minsk, last year armed with wisecracks and banter. As the special envoy to Belarus, he began building a relationship with Mr. Lukashenko over dirty jokes, vodka shots and weight-loss advice. Their rapport paved the way for Belarus to free 500 political prisoners and grant pardons for several hundred more. Its leader has also become a back channel between the United States and Russia, which is Belarus’s closest ally.

In exchange, Mr. Coale has negotiated sanctions relief for Mr. Lukashenko and has offered a road map to normalizing ties between the United States and Belarus.

“Humor is a gigantic weapon,” Mr. Coale, 79, said in a recent interview in Washington at a private club overlooking the White House. “If you can get the other guy laughing, you’re halfway there and you’re not a threat.”

Their repartee embodies Mr. Trump’s preferred personalized, deal-making approach to diplomacy. The president often sidelines career diplomats in favor of envoys like Mr. Coale, a lawyer with little previous government experience. Mr. Trump relishes the drama of high-profile prisoner exchanges and hostage releases, counting them as wins that offer a clearer narrative of success than more complex geopolitical conflicts.

Mr. Coale’s efforts have earned him attention from the president. Mr. Coale said the two have discussed expanding his mission to include liberty for political prisoners anywhere in the world. The White House declined to comment publicly.

To critics, Mr. Coale is rewarding a corrupt, authoritarian government. Some Belarusians are uncomfortable with exchanging sanctions relief for political prisoners. Activists have called the judicial system “a conveyor belt” because new political prisoners are being locked up while others are being released. Others allege that effectively trading freedom for sanctions relief “encourages human trafficking.”

Mr. Coale rejects those complaints. He said he had two goals in Belarus: to free prisoners and to get its government “to want to be in the family of nations.”

Others advocates credited Mr. Coale and the State Department for the mass prisoner releases, calling them rare achievements.

“He does tremendous work without being preoccupied about being seen negotiating with Mr. Lukashenko,” said Valery Kavaleuski, a former Belarusian diplomat and a founder of a prisoner advocacy group.

Mr. Coale, a Baltimore native, was a lawyer before he joined the Trump administration. He represented victims of the world’s worst industrial disaster, the Bhopal gas leak in 1984, and negotiated the first big settlement with Big Tobacco companies in 1997, worth $386 billion.

He was politically active, building connections with both Democrats and Republicans. He said he had been a Democrat but concluded the party moved further left than he was comfortable with. His wife, Greta Van Susteren, is a former Fox News presenter now at Newsmax TV.

After mainstream social media networks banned Mr. Trump following the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol, Mr. Coale said that several of the president’s allies, including Senator Lindsey Graham, suggested he take on Mr. Trump as a legal client. At the president’s golf club in Bedminster, N.J., Mr. Coale pitched the legal strategy that would eventually result in Meta, YouTube and X each paying tens of millions of dollars to settle lawsuits over their suspensions of Mr. Trump.

Eventually, Mr. Coale was offered a role in the administration, first as deputy envoy to Ukraine before the Belarus posting.

Home to about nine million people, Belarus is sandwiched between Russia and the European Union and is considered an important buffer zone between the two. Mr. Lukashenko’s repressive rule earned him the label of “Europe’s last dictator” from Condoleezza Rice in 2005, when she was secretary of state. Washington has not had an ambassador in Minsk since 2008.

The two countries pursued cautious engagement, including during Mr. Trump’s first term, but that halted with Mr. Lukashenko’s violent suppression of the 2020 protests. After years of isolating the strongman, Christopher W. Smith, a career diplomat widely credited for driving Washington’s re-engagement with Belarus, quietly laid the groundwork for negotiations. The first meeting with Mr. Coale, the most senior U.S. official to come to Minsk in years, was another diplomatic coup for Mr. Lukashenko.

Twenty minutes into that first encounter, Mr. Lukashenko was inveighing against European leaders who have sought to isolate him. “He was ranting and raving about them, so I said, ‘They’re a bunch of cowards,’” Mr. Coale recalled, using a more vulgar term.

“I knew that’s what he wanted to hear, something like that, to lighten everything up,” Mr. Coale added with a chuckle, explaining that his views of other European leaders are actually more nuanced.

“He loved me after that,” said Mr. Coale, who is self-deprecating and projects a friendly, unpretentious confidence. “The Europeans didn’t.”

After the E.U.-bashing, it was time to drink. Mr. Coale said he downed two shots of Mr. Lukashenko’s personal branded vodka, and then poured others on the floor to stay sober for negotiations.

After toasts, Mr. Lukashenko told Mr. Coale that in addition to releasing an American citizen whose freedom Washington had sought, he would send home another American who hadn’t been part of negotiations “because I like you.”

During a subsequent meeting in Minsk in June 2025, Mr. Lukashenko noticed that Mr. Coale had slimmed down. The American told him about Zepbound, the weight-loss jab that had helped him lose 40 pounds. He had accompanied Keith Kellogg, a retired lieutenant general and Mr. Trump’s envoy for Russia and Ukraine, and the meeting lasted more than six hours.

Shortly after, 14 political prisoners, including the husband of the opposition leader Svetlana Tikhanovskaya, were released.

Mr. Coale and Ms. Van Susteren had dinner not long after with Mr. Trump, whom they have known socially for decades. When Ms. Van Susteren told the president that her husband’s most recent visit to Belarus had resulted in 14 prisoners being freed, he insisted on talking to Mr. Lukashenko by phone. Days later, Mr. Trump called while en route to his meeting with Mr. Putin last year in Alaska and said he hoped to welcome the Belarusian leader to the White House one day.

At a penal colony in Belarus, in between sewing law enforcement uniforms and doing manual labor, Katsiaryna Andreyeva watched Mr. Coale’s visits on state television. Ms. Andreyeva, jailed for covering the 2020 protests for the Warsaw-based channel Belsat, had resigned herself to serving her two sentences totaling more than eight years. But Mr. Coale’s visits gave her some hope.

In mid-February, she was transferred to a state security services prison in Minsk. After five weeks of psychological pressure, including stints in a padded cell, she said, masked men put her into a vehicle and told the inmates to ride in silence with their heads down.

It was only when Mr. Coale, whom she had seen on television during enforced propaganda-watching sessions, threw open the doors of the prison van that she knew for sure she was free.

“You are free!” she remembered him saying. He extended his arm for a handshake. Ms. Andreyeva pulled him in for a hug.

Mr. Coale said that watching as political prisoners realized they were free was the biggest driver for him. “What motivates me is opening the doors” to vehicles carrying newly freed prisoners, he said.

He plans to leverage his relationships to help Russian political prisoners, too. Mr. Coale said he had been approached by Russian Nobel Peace Prize laureate Dmitri A. Muratov to facilitate a civilian prisoner exchange between Russia and Ukraine. While such an effort would be enormously complicated, Mr. Coale said he had received financial commitments from two organizations to resettle the prisoners elsewhere.

But first, he wants to get the rest of Belarus’s political prisoners out of jail. He was expecting, he said, another big exchange very soon.

item.title: Who Has the Last Say in Lebanon? Hezbollah and the State Both Say They Do.
item.description:
When Lebanese and Israeli officials sat down in April for their first direct talks in decades, Lebanon’s leaders called it a breakthrough: a chance, finally, to reclaim some control over the country’s fate after Hezbollah had dragged it into yet another war with Israel.

But four months and seven rounds of negotiations later, there is little to show for it. The standstill is a blow to Lebanon’s president, Joseph Aoun, who took office last year with a popular mandate to wrest power from Hezbollah.

Mr. Aoun, elected by Lebanese lawmakers, pledged to restore the state’s monopoly on arms and curtail Hezbollah’s political sway. The government he formed spent much of last year making headway on that promise, working to strip Hezbollah’s influence from the country’s international airport, the commercial port in Beirut, and the banks, all used to smuggle in weapons and cash.

When Hezbollah fired on Israel in March in solidarity with Iran, setting off another all-out war, the shortcomings of the efforts to bring the group to heel were laid bare. However much the Lebanese state had chipped away at Hezbollah’s influence, the group could still drag the country into war.

Israel insists that its forces will remain in the large swath of southern Lebanon seized in this war until Hezbollah is disarmed. On Saturday, Lebanon’s National News Agency reported a series of Israeli airstrikes and demolitions overnight and into the morning in towns and villages around the south. Israeli forces have carried out demolitions and strikes nearly daily for about four months in areas they occupy.

Hezbollah has denounced the talks, saying it will not consider surrendering its weapons until Israeli forces withdraw from Lebanese territory. And while Lebanese officials say they want to eliminate Hezbollah’s military might, the government has little ability, if any, to actually do so.

Now, after the latest round of Israeli-Lebanese talks sputtered to a close this month, there is a growing consensus that diplomacy has reached a deadlock and that, despite its sweeping promises, the Lebanese state is back to where it has been for decades: stuck.

“They are at complete loggerheads,” said Paul Salem, a nonresident senior associate with the Center for Strategic and International Studies. “It’s not a dead end, but it’s in a stalemate right now.”

For decades, Hezbollah had an iron grip on the Lebanese state. With an arsenal far greater than that of the Lebanese Army and a loyal support base among Lebanon’s Shiite Muslim community, the Iran-backed militant group served as the ultimate arbiter of power in a country whose government has been long crippled by dysfunction, corruption and political paralysis.

But after Hezbollah’s previous war with Israel ended in a cease-fire in November 2024, the group appeared battered and the country seemed exhausted. For the first time in decades, there was a groundswell of public support for reclaiming power from Hezbollah.

In the months since all-out war resumed in March, Hezbollah and the government have each sought to demonstrate that they alone really hold power in Lebanon. Each, in its own way, has tried to show who can best end the war and roll back Israel’s new occupation.

In June, the United States and Iran signed a preliminary deal to suspend their conflict, and that also included a halt to fighting in Lebanon. It was evidence, Hezbollah argued, that only its patron, Iran, could bring the war in Lebanon to an end.

The Lebanese government has since sought to demonstrate it plays the leading role, embarking on direct talks with Israeli officials. Given the countries’ long history of animosity — neither had ever formally recognized the other’s sovereignty — analysts say the meetings themselves marked a significant step forward.

“That the talks exist, that the Lebanese state and Israeli state said we want to and will continue to talk directly to each other, that’s an important thing to have in the regional toolbox,” Mr. Salem said.

The talks led the two sides to agree in principle to a phased arrangement: Israel would withdraw from pockets of southern Lebanon as the Lebanese Army moved in to secure the areas and keep Hezbollah out of them. But the initial rollout has slowed in recent weeks, with Israel refusing to expand the program further and arguing that the Lebanese Army’s efforts have fallen short.

That has left southern Lebanon trapped in the same simmering conflict it has been stuck in for months. Israeli forces have continued to demolish buildings and infrastructure in the villages they now occupy. Hezbollah has continued to fire on Israeli forces in Lebanese territory. And hundreds of thousands of Lebanese are still displaced from their homes.

“People want to move past this chapter with so many conflicts with Israel, conflicts that are seen as serving an outside agenda and not the Lebanese’ interests,” said Mohanad Hage Ali, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Middle East Center in Beirut. “But now talks have stalled, people are waiting. There was a window of opportunity that people fear is closing.”

item.title: Carney Stands Up to Trump in Trade War Despite the Risks
item.description:
On Friday night, Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada did something that few other world leaders before him have dared to do.

After days of intense trade negotiations with the United States, with less than an hour to go on a midnight deadline for a new round of tariffs from the Trump administration, Mr. Carney instructed his negotiators to walk away.

Then, he announced that once 50 percent tariffs came into effect on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods, he would order retaliatory tariffs on the United States “dollar for dollar.”

In a statement, Mr. Carney said he had gone into the trade talks in good faith, seeking “the best deal for Canadians” but “never a deal at any price or on any deadline.”

By walking away, Mr. Carney chose a road that no major U.S. ally has taken: With his country’s economy on the line, he stood up to President Trump and refused to accept the administration’s offer of a new trade relationship with tariffs permanently baked in. Britain, the European Union and other major U.S. trading partners have agreed to smaller deals that have been volatile and often left them worse off.

The collapse of the talks came after Mr. Trump declared on Tuesday that the deal was practically done.

Mr. Carney never echoed that. Over the week, as negotiators spent long hours in Washington huddled in the office of the U.S. trade representative, Mr. Carney appeared optimistic but insisted that there was still work to be done.

Until there wasn’t.

Each side now claims that the other introduced new or unreasonable demands at the last minute — the kind of finger-pointing that is common when trade talks fall apart.

Make no mistake, Mr. Carney has a lot to lose.

Canada, which is closely integrated with the United States and relies on it for defense, is heavily dependent on trade with its superpower neighbor. In his statement, Mr. Carney acknowledged the cost of his choice for many Canadians by saying that his government would work to support industries and companies affected by the new tariffs.

It will also be costly for U.S. residents, who have been paying for Mr. Trump’s tariff policies through higher prices that have also been driven by the war in Iran and spiraling oil costs.

But on Friday, Mr. Carney appeared resolved to shoulder the costs of his decision. And he has risked Mr. Trump’s ire before.

In a speech in Davos, Switzerland, in January, he described a new era in which the United States was no longer a guarantor of stability and where middle powers like Canada have to unite to survive. The speech — and its enthusiastic global reception — angered Mr. Trump.

Mr. Trump has also been riled by Mr. Carney’s outreach to China, which led to a narrow but significant trade agreement this year; by Canada’s persistence on banning the sale of U.S. liquor; and by the Carney government’s retaliatory measures against the United States for its broad, devastating tariffs on core Canadian industries.

Since he rose to lead Canada last year, Mr. Carney has put in motion a plan to help his country survive Mr. Trump’s presidency and, in the long run, thrive apart from the United States. One of his favorite lines is that “nostalgia is not a policy,” and he has told everyone who will listen that there is no going back to the old relationship with the United States — a close and familial, if lopsided, bond.

Instead, Mr. Carney has been traveling to secure new partnerships in Asia and Europe, a generational shift away from economic dependence on the United States, although that is unlikely to bear fruit fast enough to cushion the blow of the breakdown of the two countries’ relationship.

It’s likely that Mr. Trump will not take kindly to Mr. Carney’s trade decision. Just before beginning his second term, Mr. Trump said he was willing to inflict “economic pain” on Canada to get what he wanted. He has repeatedly expressed a desire to make Canada the 51st state, describing it as little more than a vassal that “lives because of the United States.”

But Mr. Carney’s vision for Canada, with a surprising assist from Mr. Trump’s needling, has ignited a wave of patriotism. Going into the trade talks, more than half of Canadians — many more than those who voted for Mr. Carney — said they wanted him to give nothing away.

Several premiers of different political stripes expressed their support for Mr. Carney after his decision. Doug Ford, a conservative who leads Ontario, cheered him on. David Eby, the progressive premier of British Columbia, said, “We didn’t ask for this, but we’ll keep fighting for as long as it takes.”

Not everyone is enthusiastic. Danielle Smith, the conservative premier of Alberta, who has good relations with the MAGA movement, was more circumspect and urged Mr. Carney to return to the negotiating table. Canada’s industry is aghast with the prolonged turbulence and uncertainty that Mr. Trump’s trade war against Canada, and Mr. Carney’s refusal to submit, are causing.

But there is little doubt that Mr. Carney will also be cheered, at home and abroad, for doing what he thought was best for his country, and for saying, in his Friday statement, that “we will not allow any nation to determine our future.”
